      <h3>Introduction</h3>
      <p>
        If your company is entering liquidation, one of the first worries you
        may have is what happens to the business assets. You might be thinking
        about equipment, stock, vehicles, or even the brand name you built.
        Many directors ask whether they can keep or repurchase these items to
        start again.
      </p>
      <p>
        This is a very common situation in UK liquidation. Wanting to retain
        useful assets or continue trading in a new structure does not create a
        problem in itself. What matters is how it is handled and whether the
        correct process is followed.
      </p>

      <h3>Understanding the Issue in Plain English</h3>
      <p>
        When a company enters liquidation, control of the company moves from
        you (the directors) to the liquidator.
      </p>
      <p>The liquidator’s job is simple:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Collect company assets</li>
        <li>Sell them for the best possible value</li>
        <li>Use the funds to pay creditors (including HMRC)</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        Those assets do not automatically disappear. They must be sold. And
        importantly, they can be sold to you, provided the sale is done
        properly and at market value.
      </p>
      <p>
        So yes, in many cases, directors can buy back assets from a liquidator.
      </p>
      <p>But the key principle is fairness.</p>
      <p>The liquidator must show that:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>The assets were valued correctly</li>
        <li>The sale achieved the best available price</li>
        <li>Creditors were treated fairly</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        This protects you and ensures the transaction cannot later be
        challenged.
      </p>

      <h3>What Directors Are Usually Worried About</h3>
      <p>Directors often fear three main things.</p>

      <h4>Personal risk</h4>
      <p>
        You may worry buying assets looks suspicious or illegal. It is not
        illegal when done correctly through a licensed liquidator.
      </p>

      <h4>Cost</h4>
      <p>
        You might assume the liquidator will refuse or price assets
        unrealistically high. In reality, the liquidator must accept reasonable
        market value, not inflated prices.
      </p>

      <h4>Losing control</h4>
      <p>
        You may feel the business disappears completely. In many cases,
        directors legally start again using purchased assets in a new company
        structure after a Creditors’ Voluntary Liquidation (CVL).
      </p>

      <h3>What UK Insolvency Rules Actually Say</h3>
      <p>
        UK insolvency rules allow directors to purchase company assets. The law
        does not prevent it. Instead, it regulates how it happens.
      </p>
      <p>The liquidator must act in the interests of creditors, not against you.</p>
      <p>The process normally involves:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Independent valuation of assets</li>
        <li>Offer to the open market if required</li>
        <li>Director offer considered equally with other buyers</li>
        <li>Sale completed at fair value</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        If your offer matches market value, the liquidator can sell to you.
        This commonly applies to:
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li>Machinery and equipment</li>
        <li>Vehicles</li>
        <li>Stock</li>
        <li>Office furniture</li>
        <li>Intellectual property</li>
        <li>Customer databases</li>
        <li>The business trading name</li>
      </ul>

      <h3>Why Market Value Matters</h3>
      <p>
        The liquidator must avoid selling assets too cheaply. If assets are
        undervalued, creditors lose money, and the transaction can be
        challenged later.
      </p>
      <p>This protects everyone involved, including you.</p>
      <p>It means:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>You cannot simply take assets</li>
        <li>But you are allowed to purchase them legitimately</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        In practice, directors frequently become the natural buyer because they
        understand the value better than outside parties.
      </p>

      <h3>Common Misunderstandings</h3>
      <p><strong>“I am not allowed to touch the assets once liquidation starts”</strong></p>
      <p>
        Not true. You must not use or remove them without permission, but you
        may legally buy them from the liquidator.
      </p>
      <p><strong>“Buying assets means I did something wrong”</strong></p>
      <p>
        Also incorrect. Many solvent and compliant directors purchase assets
        after insolvency. The process exists to preserve economic value.
      </p>
      <p><strong>“The liquidator will block me from starting again”</strong></p>
      <p>
        A liquidator does not stop you restarting a business. They only ensure
        creditors are treated fairly.
      </p>
      <p><strong>“HMRC will automatically investigate me”</strong></p>
      <p>
        HMRC is treated like any other creditor. Purchasing assets properly
        does not trigger investigation by itself.
      </p>

      <h3>Starting Again After Liquidation</h3>
      <p>In many UK liquidation cases, directors:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Close an unviable company</li>
        <li>Purchase suitable assets</li>
        <li>Start a new company structure</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        This is sometimes called a business restart or “phoenix” arrangement,
        but it is perfectly legitimate when handled transparently.
      </p>
      <p>
        The key is timing and advice before liquidation, not after problems
        arise.
      </p>

      <h3>How Easy Liquidation Helps</h3>
      <p>

      </p>

        <li>What assets you may retain</li>
        <li>How valuations work</li>
        <li>How to avoid personal risk</li>
        <li>Structuring a compliant restart if suitable</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        Everything is handled confidentially and professionally. The goal is
        clarity, not pressure.
      </p>
      <p>
        Directors often feel relief once they understand the rules properly.

      <h3>Practical Steps You Should Take Now</h3>
      <p>If your company may enter liquidation:</p>

      <h3>Quick Answer Summary</h3>
      <p>
        Yes, you can buy back and reuse your company name after liquidation, but
        you must follow strict legal procedures to avoid prosecution. You
        typically need to purchase the business assets and goodwill from the
        appointed insolvency practitioner and issue a specific statutory notice
        to creditors within 28 days.
      </p>

      <h3>Simple Explanation</h3>
      <p>
        When a limited company goes into liquidation, its legal life ends.
        However, the business brand—its name, logo, website, and customer
        reputation—often still has value.
      </p>
      <p>
        Many directors wish to restart their business using the same or a very
        similar name. This is often called a “phoenix company”.
      </p>
      <p>
        While restarting is legal, the UK government has strict rules to prevent
        directors from closing a company to avoid paying debts, only to open a
        new one with the exact same name the next day. This confuses creditors
        and customers.
      </p>
      <p>
        To stop this, there is a general ban on reusing the name. However, the
        law provides clear exceptions that allow honest directors to rescue the
        business and legally reuse the name, provided they act transparently and
        buy the assets at a fair price.
      </p>

      <h3>Legal / Official Process</h3>
      <p>
        The primary law governing this is Section 216 of the Insolvency Act
        1986.
      </p>
      <h4>The Restriction</h4>
      <p>
        Once a company enters liquidation, any person who was a director in the
        12 months prior is banned from being involved in a company with a
        “Prohibited Name” for 5 years.
      </p>
      <p>A Prohibited Name is defined as:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>The same name as the liquidated company.</li>
        <li>
          A name so similar that it suggests an association with the liquidated
          company.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h4>The Exceptions (How Easy Liquidation do it legally)</h4>
      <p>
        To reuse the name legally, you must qualify for one of the three
        statutory exceptions under the Insolvency Rules:
      </p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          <strong>Purchase from the Liquidator (Rule 22.4):</strong> You buy the
          whole or substantially the whole of the business from the liquidator.
          You must then send a formal notice to all creditors and publish it in
          the London Gazette within 28 days of completion.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Court Permission (Rule 22.3):</strong> You apply to the Court
          for permission to use the name. This application must usually be made
          within 7 days of the liquidation starting.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Existing Use (Rule 22.5):</strong> The new company has already
          been trading with that name for at least 12 months before the
          liquidation of the old company and was not dormant.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h3>Director Position</h3>
      <p>
        Reusing a name without following the correct procedure is a criminal
        offence. It is vital to understand the risks before acting.
      </p>

      <h4>Risks and Penalties</h4>
      <p>If you contravene Section 216:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          <strong>Personal Liability:</strong> You become personally liable for
          all debts of the new company. The “corporate veil” is lifted.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Criminal Record:</strong> It is a criminal offence punishable
          by a fine or imprisonment.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Disqualification:</strong> You may be banned from acting as a
          director for up to 15 years.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h4>Common Misunderstandings</h4>
      <p>
        <strong>“I changed one word”:</strong> Simply adding “UK” or “Services”
        to the end of the old name does not work. If the name suggests an
        association, it is prohibited.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>“My accountant said it’s fine”:</strong> General accountants
        often miss the nuances of insolvency law. Only a licensed insolvency
        practitioner can guide this sale safely.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>“Nobody will check”:</strong> Creditors and HMRC actively
        monitor for phoenix companies. If the new company fails, the liquidator
        will investigate the name usage immediately.
      </p>

      <h3>Eligibility Rules</h3>
      <p>Can you reuse your company name? Use this logic to check your position:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          IF you buy the business assets from the liquidator AND publish a
          Gazette notice within 28 days → THEN you may reuse the name legally.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF you apply to Court for permission within 7 days of liquidation →
          THEN you may continue using the name while the court decides (up to 6
          weeks).
        </li>
        <li>
          IF you have another company that has traded with that name for over 12
          months → THEN you may usually continue using it.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF you simply register a new company with a similar name without
          buying assets → THEN you are likely breaking the law (Section 216).
        </li>
        <li>
          IF the name is distinct and completely unrelated → THEN Section 216
          does not apply.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h3>How This Connects to Insolvency Options</h3>
      <p>
        The ability to reuse a name is tightly linked to the liquidation
        process. You cannot buy the name back if the company is merely “struck
        off” or dissolved; it must go through a formal liquidation process
        where assets are valued and sold.
      </p>
      <p>
        This is most relevant during a Creditors’ Voluntary Liquidation (CVL).
        In this process, the director acknowledges the company cannot pay its
        debts but acts responsibly to close it.
      </p>
      <p>
        By working with a licensed insolvency practitioner, you arrange for the
        valuation of the company’s goodwill (the value of the name and
        reputation). You then pay this value into the liquidation pot for the
        benefit of the creditors. This transforms an insolvent company problem
        into a legitimate business rescue, protecting you from personal
        liability.
      </p>
      <p>
        If you are considering closing your business but want to restart, you
        should review our Company Liquidation Services to understand how the
        asset sale fits into the timeline.
      </p>
      <h3>Step-by-Step Actions (What To Do Next)</h3>
      <p>
        If you intend to restart your business using the same name, follow this
        sequence:
      </p>
      <ol>
        <li>
          <strong>Consult an Insolvency Practitioner (IP):</strong> Do this
          before you take any action. Explain your intention to buy the business
          back.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Get Professional Valuations:</strong> An independent agent
          must value the company assets and goodwill (the name). You cannot just
          make up a price.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Enter Liquidation:</strong> The insolvency practitioner places
          the old company into liquidation.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Purchase the Assets:</strong> You pay the agreed valuation
          price to the liquidator for the assets and name.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Issue Statutory Notices:</strong> Your solicitor or insolvency
          practitioner will draft a specific notice (Rule 22.4 Notice).
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Publish in the Gazette:</strong> This notice must appear in
          the London Gazette within 28 days of the purchase.
        </li>
        <li>
          <strong>Notify Creditors:</strong> Send the same notice to every
          creditor of the old company.
        </li>
      </ol>
     
      <h3>Practical Real-World Scenarios</h3>
      <h4>Scenario A: The Small Trade Restart</h4>
      <p>
        <strong>Situation:</strong> A plumbing firm, "Smith &amp; Sons Heating
        Ltd," goes bust. Mr. Smith wants to start "Smith &amp; Sons Repairs
        Ltd."
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>Outcome:</strong> The names are too similar. Mr. Smith buys the
        van and tools from the liquidator. He must also pay for the "goodwill"
        of the name and publish a Gazette notice. If he fails to publish the
        notice, he becomes personally liable for the new company's debts.
      </p>
      <h4>Scenario B: The Tech Startup (Intangible Assets)</h4>
      <p>
        <strong>Situation:</strong> A software company fails. The value is
        entirely in the code and the brand name "TechFlow."
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>Outcome:</strong> The director buys the intellectual property
        rights and the brand "TechFlow" from the liquidator. Because there are
        no physical assets, the valuation focuses on the brand. The director
        follows the notification rules and successfully restarts.
      </p>
      <h4>Scenario C: The HMRC Flag</h4>
      <p>
        <strong>Situation:</strong> A director closes a marketing agency owing
        £50,000 to HMRC. She opens a new agency with the same name the next day
        without buying the assets or notifying anyone.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>Outcome:</strong> The director would not be personally liable 
        for the £50,000 debt of the old company purely because of the name reuse. 
        At Easy Liquidation, our advice is highly valuable in situations like this.
         Taking early professional guidance can help you avoid breaching the rules, 
         protect yourself from personal liability, and ensure the correct legal process is followed.
      </p>
     
      <h3>How Easy Liquidation Can Help</h3>
      <p>
        Dealing with a failed business is stressful, but wanting to preserve

      <p>

      </p>
      <p>We ensure:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Accurate valuation of goodwill.</li>
        <li>Correct legal notices are drafted.</li>
        <li>You are fully protected from personal liability claims.</li>
        <li>The restart is compliant and transparent to creditors.</li>
      </ul>
      
      <h3>FAQs</h3>
      <h4>How much does it cost to buy back my company name?</h4>
      <p>
        The cost depends on the independent valuation of the goodwill. It is not
        a fixed fee; it reflects what the name is worth in the open market.
      </p>
      <h4>Can I just change the name slightly?</h4>
      <p>
        No. If the new name suggests an association with the old company (for
        example, "ABC Trading Ltd" to "ABC Services Ltd"), it is still a
        prohibited name.
      </p>
      <h4>What happens if I don't publish the Gazette notice?</h4>
      <p>
        You lose the legal protection of the exception. You will be personally
        liable for the debts of the new company and may face criminal
        prosecution.
      </p>
      <h4>Can I be a director of the new company?</h4>
      <p>
        Yes, provided you are not currently disqualified and you follow the
        Section 216 exceptions (purchase and notification) correctly.
      </p>
      <h4>How long does the ban on the name last?</h4>
      <p>
        The restriction on using a prohibited name lasts for 5 years from the
        date the company went into liquidation.
      </p>

    content: `
      
      <p>
        When a company has no money to pay redundancy, employees can claim
        statutory redundancy pay from the government's Redundancy Payments
        Service, which is part of the Insolvency Service. Payments are made from
        the National Insurance Fund and cover redundancy pay, unpaid wages,
        holiday pay, and notice pay up to statutory limits.
      </p>
      <h3>How Redundancy Works When Your Company Has No Money</h3>
      <p>
        You might assume that if the company is broke, nobody gets paid. That is
        not how it works.
      </p>
      <p>
        When an employer is insolvent and unable to make redundancy payments,
        the government steps in through the Redundancy Payments Service. The
        money does not come from your company. It comes from the National
        Insurance Fund.
      </p>
      <p>
        This means staff get their statutory entitlements even when the business
        has nothing left.
      </p>
      <p>
        The system exists because the government recognises that employees
        should not be left penniless when a company fails. You and your staff
        have contributed to National Insurance throughout your employment. This
        fund protects you when things go wrong.
      </p>
      <h3>What Is the Redundancy Payments Service?</h3>
      <p>
        The Redundancy Payments Service is a government service you use to claim
        money if your employer owes you redundancy payment or other money like
        wages, holiday and commission when your employer is unable to pay
        because they're insolvent.
      </p>
      <p>
        The service processes claims quickly. In the last year, the Insolvency
        Service efficiently processed 69,237 redundancy payments.
      </p>
      <p>
        You apply online. The insolvency practitioner handling your company's
        liquidation will give you the reference number you need to make your
        claim.
      </p>
      <p>
        The government pays you directly. Your former company does not handle
        any of this.
      </p>
      <h3>Can Directors Claim Redundancy Pay?</h3>
      <p>Yes. Many directors do not realise this.</p>
      <p>
        Directors can claim redundancy pay if they are also employees of the
        company with a contract of employment that outlines their duties and
        responsibilities. Being a director alone is not enough. You must also be
        an employee.
      </p>
      <p>You qualify if:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>You have a formal employment contract (written, oral, or implied).</li>
        <li>You have worked for at least two continuous years.</li>
        <li>Your role as a director was active rather than purely office holding.</li>
        <li>You were paid via PAYE.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Common misconceptions:</p>
      <p>
        <strong>"I own the company so I cannot claim"</strong> – Wrong.
        Ownership does not disqualify you.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>"I am the only director so it does not count"</strong> – Wrong.
        Even as the sole director, you may still be eligible if you meet the
        criteria of being an employee.
      </p>
      <p>
        <strong>"Directors are not employees"</strong> – Wrong. A director who
        is an office holder can also be an employee and be eligible for payment.
      </p>
      <p>
        The key issue is whether you worked as an employee. Your contract should
        detail the terms of your employment including salary, duties, and
        working hours.
      </p>
      <p>
        Directors must be able to prove they had more than just an advisory or
        non-executive role in the running of the business. If you turned up to
        work, did the day-to-day tasks, and drew a salary through PAYE, you were
        an employee.
      </p>
      <h3>Who Is Eligible and How Much Can You Claim?</h3>
      <p>Basic eligibility rules:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          IF you have worked for 2+ years as an employee → THEN you can claim
          statutory redundancy pay.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF the company is insolvent → THEN claims go through the Redundancy
          Payments Service.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF the company is solvent → THEN the company must pay redundancy
          directly.
        </li>
      </ul>
      <p>Payment amounts:</p>
      <p>
        If you were made redundant on or after 6 April 2025, your weekly pay is
        capped at £719. The maximum total of statutory redundancy payments you
        can get is £21,570.
      </p>
      <p>Your redundancy pay depends on your age and length of service:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Under 22: Half a week's pay for each full year.</li>
        <li>Age 22 to 40: One week's pay for each full year.</li>
        <li>Age 41 and over: One and a half weeks' pay for each full year.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Service is capped at 20 years maximum.</p>
      <p>Other payments you can claim:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          Redundancy pay (if employed for at least two years).
        </li>
        <li>
          Unpaid wages (including overtime, bonuses, or commission).
        </li>
        <li>
          Holiday pay (for any annual leave owed but not paid).
        </li>
        <li>
          Statutory notice pay (if you worked for at least one month).
        </li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        For redundancy pay, arrears of pay and notice pay, if your number of
        hours worked per week varied, an average is taken across 12 weeks. For
        holiday pay, if your number of hours worked per week varied, an average
        is taken over 52 weeks.
      </p>
      <p>Maximum amounts:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Unpaid wages: up to 8 weeks.</li>
        <li>Holiday pay: up to 6 weeks.</li>
        <li>Notice pay: up to 12 weeks.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        If you are owed more than the maximum the government can pay, you can
        register as a creditor in the insolvency for any outstanding money
        you're owed.
      </p>
      <h3>What Happens During Liquidation?</h3>
      <p>When your company enters liquidation, the process moves quickly.</p>
      <p>Typical timeline:</p>
      <ol>
        <li>Company enters formal insolvency (liquidation or administration).</li>
        <li>An insolvency practitioner is appointed.</li>
        <li>Staff are made redundant.</li>
        <li>The insolvency practitioner issues case reference numbers.</li>
        <li>Employees submit claims online.</li>
        <li>The government processes claims.</li>
        <li>Payments are made directly to claimants.</li>
      </ol>
      <p>
        Claims for redundancy payments should usually be made within six months
        of the date of liquidation, although this can be extended to 12 months
        in some cases.
      </p>
      <p>
        You can only apply after the official date of insolvency, which will be
        confirmed by the insolvency practitioner managing the case.
      </p>
      <p>
        The insolvency practitioner will provide you with the forms and
        guidance. You might receive multiple payments as each claim type is
        processed.
      </p>
      <p>
        When you're going through company liquidation, your insolvency
        practitioner will explain how redundancy claims fit into the wider
        process and ensure you receive everything you're entitled to claim.
      </p>
      <h3>What You Should Do Next</h3>
      <h4>Step 1: Speak to a licensed insolvency practitioner</h4>
      <p>
        Get clear advice on whether liquidation is the right option. They will
        explain the process and your entitlements.
      </p>
      <h4>Step 2: Gather your employment records</h4>
      <p>
        Collect your employment contract, payslips, P60s, and any documents
        showing your role and salary. Directors applying to the Redundancy
        Payments Service for monies owed will need to provide evidence to
        support their claim that they were an employee, including employment
        details, dates employed, and how much they were paid.
      </p>
      <h4>Step 3: Start formal insolvency proceedings</h4>
      <p>
        Your company must be in a formal insolvent liquidation process such as a
        Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation before you can claim redundancy pay.
        You cannot claim while the company is still trading.
      </p>
      <h4>Step 4: Work with the insolvency practitioner</h4>
      <p>
        They will provide your case reference number and help you complete the
        claim forms correctly.
      </p>
      <h4>Step 5: Submit your claims online</h4>
      <p>
        Use the Redundancy Payments Service website. You will need separate
        claims for redundancy pay and notice pay.
      </p>
      <h4>Step 6: Wait for payment</h4>
      <p>
        The Insolvency Service will contact you if further information is
        needed. It is recommended to wait at least six weeks before checking on
        progress.
      </p>
      <h4>Step 7: Register as a creditor for any excess</h4>
      <p>
        If you are owed more than the statutory caps, register your additional
        claim with the insolvency practitioner.
      </p>
      <h3>Real-World Scenarios</h3>
      <h4>Scenario 1: Small retail business</h4>
      <p>
        Sarah runs a clothing shop. She has three staff and has been trading for
        six years. The business cannot pay its debts.
      </p>
      <p>
        Sarah closes the shop and appoints a liquidator. All four people
        (including Sarah as director) are made redundant. Each person worked for
        more than two years and was paid via PAYE.
      </p>
      <p>
        All four submit claims to the Redundancy Payments Service. Sarah
        receives £8,640 in redundancy pay based on her age and service. Her
        staff receive payments ranging from £4,000 to £7,000. Nobody waited for
        the company to somehow find money it did not have.
      </p>
      <h4>Scenario 2: Limited company contractor</h4>
      <p>
        James operates as a one-person limited company doing IT contracting.
        After five years, work dries up. The company owes £15,000 to HMRC and
        suppliers.
      </p>
      <p>
        James wonders if he can claim redundancy as the only employee. He can.
        He has an employment contract, took a salary through PAYE, and worked
        for over two years.
      </p>
      <p>
        He liquidates the company and claims redundancy pay of £10,800 plus
        unpaid wages and holiday pay. The money comes from the government, not
        from his insolvent company.
      </p>
      <h4>Scenario 3: Family business with director shareholders</h4>
      <p>
        Two brothers run a building firm as directors and equal shareholders.
        They have five employees. The company becomes insolvent with £80,000 in
        debts.
      </p>
      <p>
        Both directors qualify for redundancy because they have employment
        contracts and work full-time in the business. They are not excluded
        simply because they own shares.
      </p>
      <p>
        All seven people claim redundancy. The employees receive their statutory
        payments. The two directors each receive around £12,000 based on their
        service and age. Everyone is paid by the government.
      </p>

      <h3>Frequently Asked Questions</h3>
      <h4>Can I claim redundancy if the company is still trading?</h4>
      <p>
        No. Claims cannot be made during a Members' Voluntary Liquidation as
        this process is for solvent companies. The company must be insolvent and
        in a formal insolvency process before claims can be submitted.
      </p>
      <h4>What if I do not have a written employment contract?</h4>
      <p>
        While not mandatory, having a written contract significantly strengthens
        your case. If you lack a formal agreement, you must provide other
        evidence of an employment relationship such as consistent work patterns
        and responsibilities. Payslips showing PAYE, P60s, and evidence of your
        working role all help prove employee status.
      </p>
      <h4>Will claiming redundancy affect my credit rating?</h4>
      <p>
        No. Receiving redundancy payments does not affect your personal credit
        rating. You are claiming a statutory entitlement, not declaring personal
        insolvency.
      </p>
      <h4>How long does it take to receive payment?</h4>
      <p>

      </p>
      <h4>What happens if my claim is rejected?</h4>
      <p>
        If your claim is rejected, you can take your employer to an employment
        tribunal to show you were redundant. You must start the process of
        applying to the tribunal within 6 months minus 1 day from when your
        employment ended. Your insolvency practitioner can guide you through
        this process.

      <h3>Quick Answer</h3>
      <p>
        Yes, in most cases you can start a new company after liquidation. Being a
        director of a company that goes into liquidation does not automatically
        prevent you from running another business. However, there are strict
        legal rules you must follow, particularly around using the same or a
        substantially similar company name.
      </p>
      <p>
        If you are disqualified as a director, you cannot legally act as a
        director of any new company or be involved in its formation or
        management during the disqualification period. If you follow the rules,
        starting again is entirely possible and many directors do so
        successfully.
      </p>

      <h3>What Does Liquidation Mean for Your Future?</h3>
      <p>
        Liquidation closes your company; it should not prevent you from earning
        a living from your chosen career.
      </p>
      <p>
        Many directors who go through a Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation
        (CVL) or compulsory liquidation go on to start new businesses. The law
        does not punish honest failure. What it does punish is dishonest
        conduct, ignoring director duties, or attempting to avoid your
        obligations by simply starting again under a different name.
      </p>
      <p>
        The key question is not whether you can start again. The key question
        is what changes you would bring this time and whether anything from the
        liquidation creates a legal barrier to doing so and, if so, what that
        barrier is.
      </p>
      <p>There are three main areas to understand:</p>
      <ol>
        <li>
          The Prohibited Name Rule — restrictions on reusing your old company
          name
        </li>
        <li>
          Director disqualification — when you are disqualified from acting as
          director of a UK company
        </li>
        <li>
          The “Phoenix Company” Rules — HMRC and the Insolvency Service's
          approach to serial insolvency
        </li>
      </ol>

      <h3>The Prohibited Name Rule — Section 216</h3>
      <p>This is the rule that catches most directors by surprise.</p>
      <p>
        Section 216 of the Insolvency Act 1986 makes it a criminal offence to
        be involved in the formation or management of a company that uses a
        name which is the same as, or so substantially similar to, the name of
        an insolvent company you were a director of, where people may not
        appreciate the new business is a separate legal entity in providing
        credit terms. The prohibition is for a period of five years after the
        liquidation.
      </p>
      <p>
        This applies to you if you were a director of the company in the 12
        months before it went into liquidation.
      </p>

      <h4>What counts as a prohibited name?</h4>
      <p>A prohibited name is:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          Any name by which the company was known at any time in the 12 months
          before it went into liquidation — this includes both its registered
          company name and any trading names/styles used
        </li>
        <li>
          Any name that is so substantially similar to that name that it could
          suggest an association with the liquidated company
        </li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        This means the restriction is not limited to the exact company name. It
        also captures names that may give the impression the new business is a
        continuation of, or connected to, the old one, even if the wording is
        slightly different.
      </p>

      <h4>Example</h4>
      <p>
        If your old company was called “Northern Contracts Ltd”, you cannot then
        set up or manage a company called “Northern Contracts (2024) Ltd” or
        trade under the name “Northern Contracts” without following the correct
        legal process.
      </p>

      <h4>What happens if you break this rule?</h4>
      <ul>
        <li>
          It is a criminal offence carrying up to two years in prison and/or an
          unlimited fine
        </li>
        <li>
          You can be held personally liable for the debts of the new company,
          should that company later fail/run into issues
        </li>
        <li>
          The Insolvency Service is actively increasing enforcement in this
          area. In the November 2025 Budget, the Government announced a new
          Abusive Phoenixism Taskforce within the Insolvency Service, which is
          being established from 2026 and will be staffed by around 50
          investigators to target directors who abuse insolvency processes to
          avoid debts.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h4>The exceptions — when you can legally reuse the name</h4>
      <p>
        There are three legal routes that allow you to use a prohibited name,
        but each has strict conditions.
      </p>
      <p><strong>Exception 1 — Court Permission</strong></p>
      <p>
        You apply to court for permission to use the name. The court considers
        whether it is just and equitable to allow it. This process takes time
        and requires legal support.
      </p>
      <p><strong>Exception 2 — The Business Was Sold</strong></p>
      <p>
        If the whole or substantially the whole of the business is acquired
        from a liquidator, administrator or supervisor, and notice is given to
        creditors and published in the Gazette within 28 days, prior to reuse
        of the name, the name may be reused.
      </p>
      <p><strong>Exception 3 — The Name Was Already Being Used</strong></p>
      <p>
        If the new company has been trading and using the prohibited name for at
        least 12 months prior to the liquidation, and has been known to the
        public under that name continuously during that period, you may be
        exempt. Dormant companies using the prohibited name will not count —
        trade must be evidenced.
      </p>
      <p>
        In all cases, if you want to use a similar name, take legal advice
        before doing so.
      </p>

      <h3>Director Disqualification — What It Means</h3>
      <p>
        Director disqualification does not happen automatically. It only arises
        if misconduct is found following investigation.
      </p>
      <p>
        Following a CVL or compulsory liquidation, the appointed insolvency
        practitioner (in a CVL) or the Official Receiver is required to report
        on your conduct as a director. This report goes to the Insolvency
        Service.
      </p>
      <p>
        If the Insolvency Service decides your conduct falls below the standard
        expected of a director, it can apply to court for a disqualification
        order, or invite you to enter a disqualification undertaking.
      </p>
      <p>
        Disqualification periods range from 2 to 15 years depending on the
        seriousness of the conduct.
      </p>

      <h4>What type of conduct can lead to disqualification?</h4>
      <ul>
        <li>Trading while knowingly insolvent and causing further losses to creditors</li>
        <li>Failing to keep proper accounting records</li>
        <li>
          Making preference payments — paying connected parties ahead of the
          general trade creditors and HMRC
        </li>
        <li>Taking excessive director drawings when the company was insolvent</li>
        <li>
          Misusing Bounce Back Loans or COVID support funding including recovery
          loans
        </li>
        <li>Dissolving a company to avoid paying debts</li>
      </ul>

      <h4>What disqualification means in practice</h4>
      <p>If you are disqualified, you cannot legally:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Act as a director of any company registered in the UK</li>
        <li>Be involved in the management of a company, even without the title of director</li>
        <li>Promote, form, or manage a limited liability partnership (LLP)</li>
      </ul>
      <p>Acting while disqualified is a criminal offence.</p>
      <p><strong>What disqualification does not prevent you from doing:</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          You can still work for yourself or operate as a sole trader (subject
          to any separate bankruptcy restrictions)
        </li>
        <li>
          You can become a director again once your disqualification period has
          ended — your rights are fully restored at that point
        </li>
      </ul>
      <p>
        If you behaved honestly, cooperated fully with the liquidator, and
        followed your director duties, disqualification is unlikely. Most
        directors who go through a straightforward CVL are not disqualified.
      </p>

      <h3>The Phoenix Company Rules — HMRC and the Insolvency Service</h3>
      <p>
        A “phoenix company” is a term commonly used to describe a new business
        that continues the trade of a previous company following insolvency,
        often involving the same directors, staff, customers, premises, or
        business model.
      </p>
      <p>
        Phoenixing is not illegal; in many cases, it is entirely legitimate for
        a director to purchase the assets of an insolvent company from a
        liquidator at fair market value and continue trading through a new
        company, provided this is done transparently and in accordance with
        insolvency law.
      </p>
      <p>
        What the law does prohibit is abusive phoenixing, where a director
        deliberately misuses the insolvency process. This can include allowing
        debts to build up without intention to repay, transferring assets out
        of a failing company at undervalue, or repeatedly liquidating companies
        to avoid liabilities and then continuing the same business.
      </p>
      <p>
        HMRC also has powers, in certain circumstances, to make directors
        personally liable for company tax debts, particularly in cases involving
        repeated insolvency or deliberate tax avoidance. These powers have been
        strengthened in recent years.
      </p>
      <p>
        The key principle is clear: starting again is permitted, but it must be
        done properly and transparently.
      </p>

      <h3>Decision Rules — What Applies to Your Situation</h3>
      <ul>
        <li>
          IF you were a director of a company that went into liquidation → You
          can generally start a new company, provided you are not disqualified
          and you comply with the prohibited name rules under Section 216 of the
          Insolvency Act 1986 and Part 22 of the Insolvency Rules 1986.

      <h3>How This Connects to Your Insolvency Options</h3>
      <h4>Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)</h4>
      <p>
        A CVL is the legally correct way to close an insolvent company. It is
        director-led, which means you control the timing and the process. It
        also places you in the best possible position to start again because
        you acted responsibly.
      </p>
      <h4>Compulsory Liquidation</h4>
      <p>
        If you wait for HMRC or another creditor to obtain a winding up order,

      </p>
      <h4>Dissolution</h4>
      <p>

        debts. Directors who dissolved companies with Bounce Back Loans or HMRC

      </p>

      <h3>What to Do Right Now</h3>
      <ol>

        <li>

    title: "What Happens When You Receive a Winding Up Petition?",
    excerpt: "If a creditor, for example HMRC, has served you with a winding up petition, your company faces being forcibly closed by a court unless you act within days. Once the petition is advertised in the London Gazette, it is likely that your bank accounts will be frozen.",
    imageUrl: "/what-happens-when-you-receive-a-winding-up-petition.jpg",
    content: `
      <h3>Quick Answer</h3>
      <p>
        If a creditor, for example HMRC, has served you with a winding up
        petition, your company faces being forcibly closed by a court unless you
        act within days. Once the petition is advertised in the London Gazette,
        it is likely that your bank accounts will be frozen. You have a very
        short window — often seven to ten working days — to pay the debt,
        negotiate a Time to Pay arrangement, or place the company into a formal
        insolvency process. Doing nothing will result in a compulsory
        liquidation order and complete loss of control over the business.
      </p>

      <h3>What Is a Winding Up Petition?</h3>
      <p>
        A winding up petition is a legal application made to the court asking a
        judge to forcibly close your company because it cannot pay its debts.
      </p>
      <p>
        As an example, HMRC might use this process when a company owes unpaid
        tax and has not responded to earlier demands. This includes unpaid VAT,
        PAYE, Corporation Tax, or National Insurance Contributions.
      </p>
      <p>
        HMRC is currently the UK's most active petitioner. It files more
        winding up petitions than any other creditor in England and Wales.
      </p>
      <p>
        Once a petition is presented to the court, the legal process moves
        quickly. The consequences for your company and your personal position as
        a director are serious.
      </p>

      <h3>What Happens After You Receive the Petition</h3>
      <h4>Stage 1 — Petition Served</h4>
      <p>
        Creditor's solicitors deliver legal documents to your company's
        registered address. The clock starts immediately.
      </p>
      <h4>Stage 2 — Gazetting</h4>
      <p>
        The petition is advertised in the London Gazette. This must happen at
        least seven working days after service and at least seven working days
        before the court hearing.
      </p>
      <h4>Stage 3 — Bank Accounts Frozen</h4>
      <p>
        Banks review the London Gazette for notices relating to its customers;
        when your bank sees the Gazette notice, it is likely to freeze your
        company accounts. This is automatic. You will not receive advance
        warning. It can be very difficult to trade normally after this point.
      </p>
      <h4>Stage 4 — Court Hearing</h4>
      <p>
        A judge decides whether to grant a winding up order. This typically
        takes place seven to eight weeks after the petition is presented.
      </p>
      <h4>Stage 5 — Winding Up Order</h4>
      <p>
        If the court grants the order, your company enters compulsory
        liquidation immediately and you lose all control.
      </p>
      <h4>Stage 6 — Official Receiver Appointed</h4>
      <p>
        The Official Receiver, a government-appointed insolvency official, takes
        over the company, investigates the conduct of all directors, and begins
        realising assets for creditors — usually by way of a sale.
      </p>

      <h3>The Legal Process</h3>
      <p>
        Under the Insolvency Act 1986, any creditor owed £750 or more can apply
        to court to wind up a company that cannot pay its debts.
      </p>
      <p>
        Before reaching this point, a creditor will normally have issued earlier
        warnings, including payment demands, reminder letters, a formal statutory
        demand (a 21-day written payment notice), and, in the case of HMRC,
        correspondence from their Debt Management team.
      </p>
      <p>
        If these earlier warnings and demands do not result in payment or an
        agreed arrangement, the creditor instructs its solicitors to present the
        petition at the High Court.
      </p>
      <p>
        Once a winding up order is made, the Official Receiver becomes
        liquidator. A licensed insolvency practitioner may later be appointed in
        their place. All company assets are realised and distributed to
        creditors in the legally defined order of priority.
      </p>

      <h3>Your Position as a Director</h3>
      <p>
        Receiving a petition does not automatically mean you have done something
        wrong. Many directors face petitions through genuine financial
        difficulty, not misconduct.
      </p>
      <p>
        However, the moment your company becomes insolvent, your legal duties
        change. You must now act in the interests of creditors, not shareholders
        and not yourself.
      </p>

      <p>Your risks include:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          Personal liability if you continue trading and increase losses to
          creditors
        </li>
        <li>
          Personal liability if you made preference payments — for example,
          repaying loans to yourself or family members ahead of creditors such as
          HMRC
        </li>
        <li>
          Director disqualification of between 2 and 15 years if the Official
          Receiver finds evidence of misconduct
        </li>
        <li>
          A formal investigation into your conduct in the period leading up to
          insolvency
        </li>
      </ul>

      <p>Your protections include:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>
          Acting quickly and taking professional advice is viewed positively by
          the courts and the Official Receiver
        </li>
        <li>
          Placing the company into a voluntary insolvency process gives you far
          more control than waiting for compulsory liquidation
        </li>
        <li>
          Personal liability does not automatically follow company insolvency —
          it only arises from specific wrongful acts
        </li>
      </ul>

      <p>Common misunderstandings:</p>
      <ul>
        <li>Ignoring the petition does not make it go away. It accelerates the process.</li>
        <li>
          Paying yourself or a connected party before the company enters
          insolvency can be treated as a preference payment and reversed.
        </li>
        <li>
          You cannot dissolve or strike off the company once a petition has been
          presented. Attempting to do so could be treated as misconduct.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h3>Decision Rules — What Applies to Your Situation</h3>
      <ul>
        <li>
          IF your company can pay the full debt → Pay immediately and apply to
          have the petition withdrawn before it is advertised in the Gazette.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF your company cannot pay in full but the business is viable → Urgently
          explore a Time to Pay arrangement (in the case of an HMRC debt), or
          seek advice from an Insolvency Practitioner as to whether you are in a
          position to consider a Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA).
        </li>
        <li>
          IF your company is insolvent and cannot be rescued → Speak with an
          Insolvency Practitioner to see whether the company can enter a
          Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL) before the court hearing to
          retain control and close the company properly.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF the petition has already been advertised in the Gazette → Your bank
          accounts may already be frozen. Seek advice from an Insolvency
          Practitioner immediately. Options narrow fast.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF the debt is disputed → Apply to court urgently to have the petition
          dismissed. Legal advice is essential in this situation.
        </li>
        <li>
          IF you do nothing → A winding up order will be granted. The Official
          Receiver takes control. You face a formal conduct investigation with no
          ability to influence the outcome.
        </li>
      </ul>

      <h3>How This Connects to Your Insolvency Options</h3>
      <p>
        A winding up petition does not always mean the end. There are several
        routes available depending on your position.
      </p>

      <h4>Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)</h4>
      <p>
        If the company is insolvent and cannot be saved, a CVL allows directors
        to close it in an orderly way before the court forces the issue. It
        gives you control over the timing, protects your position as a director,
        and ensures employees can access redundancy payments through the
        government's Redundancy Payments Service.
      </p>
      <p>
        At Easy Liquidation, we offer a simple, guided CVL process designed to
        make company closure as straightforward as possible. We handle the
        entire process for you and make sure you understand every step before it
        happens.
      </p>

      <h4>Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA)</h4>
      <p>
        If the business is viable but struggling with debt, a CVA allows you to
        agree a formal repayment schedule with HMRC and other creditors,
        typically over three to five years. The company continues trading while
        debts are repaid in manageable instalments.
      </p>

      <h4>Administration</h4>
      <p>
        Administration places the company under the legal protection of a
        licensed insolvency practitioner, halting the petition process
        immediately. It creates breathing space to explore a rescue, restructure,
        or sale of the business.
      </p>

      <h4>Time to Pay Arrangement</h4>
      <p>
        HMRC can agree to withdraw a petition if a full Time to Pay arrangement
        is agreed before the hearing. Once a petition has been presented,
        HMRC's requirements become significantly more demanding than at the
        initial debt stage.
      </p>

      <p>
        Our liquidation and company closure service covers all of these options
        in detail. If you are unsure which route is right for you, our team will
        walk you through each one clearly.
      </p>

      <h3>What to Do Right Now</h3>
      <ol>
        <li>Do not ignore the petition. Every day of delay reduces your options.</li>
        <li>
          Check the London Gazette immediately. Search your company name at
          thegazette.co.uk to find out whether the petition has already been
          advertised.
        </li>
        <li>
          Do not make payments to yourself, family members, or connected parties.
          These may be classed as preference payments and reversed by a
          liquidator.
        </li>
        <li>
          Do not attempt to dissolve or strike off the company. This is not
          legally permitted once a petition has been presented.
        </li>
        <li>
          Contact a licensed insolvency practitioner immediately. The sooner
          they review your position, the more options remain available.
        </li>
        <li>
          Gather your key financial documents. You will need: a list of creditors
          and amounts owed, recent bank statements, the latest company accounts,
          and all HMRC correspondence.
        </li>
        <li>
          In the case of an HMRC petition, call the Business Payment Support
          Service if the petition has not yet been advertised. There may still
          be scope to agree a Time to Pay arrangement and prevent gazetting.
        </li>
      </ol>

      <h3>Real-World Scenarios</h3>
      <h4>Scenario 1 — Small construction company</h4>
      <p>
        A small construction firm accumulated £38,000 in unpaid VAT during a
        difficult trading period. HMRC issued a statutory demand which the
        director ignored, hoping new contracts would resolve the problem. A
        petition was presented and advertised in the Gazette. The bank froze all
        company accounts that same morning, making it impossible to pay wages or
        suppliers. The director contacted Easy Liquidation the following day. A
        CVL was arranged before the court hearing, protecting the director
        personally and ensuring employees could claim redundancy through the
        Insolvency Service.
      </p>

      <h4>Scenario 2 — Director with a recoverable business</h4>
      <p>
        A retail business director received a petition for £52,000 in PAYE and
        NIC arrears. The business was still generating revenue and had a solid
        customer base. An insolvency practitioner reviewed the finances quickly
        and presented a CVA proposal to HMRC showing the debt could be repaid
        over 48 months from trading income. HMRC agreed to withdraw the petition
        and support the CVA. The business continued trading and the debt was
        cleared within four years.
      </p>

      <h4>Scenario 3 — Director concerned about personal liability</h4>
      <p>
        A consultancy director had repaid a £20,000 personal loan she had made
        to the company, three months before the HMRC petition arrived. She was
        worried this would make her personally liable for the company's
        debts. On professional advice, she disclosed the repayment fully to the
        appointed liquidator. Because it occurred within the two-year preference
        window and she was a connected party, the liquidator pursued recovery,
        but her full cooperation and transparency prevented further personal
        sanctions or disqualification.
      </p>

      <h3>How We Can Help</h3>
      <p>
        Receiving a winding up petition is frightening. Most directors who call
        us have never faced this situation before and do not know how much time
        they have or what their options are.
      </p>
      <p>
        Speaking to our team does not commit you to anything. It gives you a
        clear picture of where you stand, what routes are available, and which
        option makes the most sense for your personal position, not just the
        company.
      </p>
      <p>
        We explain everything plainly. We tell you what is likely to happen,
        what your exposure is, and what steps will protect you best. If the
        right answer is an easy liquidation through a CVL, we make the entire
        process straightforward and manageable. If there is a way to save the
        business, we will identify it.
      </p>
      <p>
        Our initial call is completely free and fully confidential. The sooner
        you speak to us, the more options you will have.
      </p>

      <h3>Frequently Asked Questions</h3>
      <h4>How long do I have after receiving a winding up petition?</h4>
      <p>
        The petition must be advertised in the Gazette at least seven working
        days after service and seven working days before the hearing. In
        practice this means you have around two to three weeks before the court
        date, but the critical deadline is before gazetting, when your bank will
        freeze your accounts. You should act within 48 hours of receiving the
        petition.
      </p>
      <h4>Will my bank account definitely be frozen?</h4>
      <p>
        Yes, in almost all cases. Once the petition appears in the London
        Gazette, your bank is legally required to freeze the company accounts.
        This happens automatically and without advance warning from the bank. It
        is one of the most immediate and damaging consequences of the petition
        process.
      </p>
      <h4>Can the creditor withdraw the petition?</h4>
      <p>
        Yes. A creditor, such as HMRC, can withdraw the petition if you pay the
        debt in full, agree a formal Time to Pay arrangement, or enter a formal
        insolvency process such as a CVL or CVA. The later you leave it, the
        harder and more expensive achieving a withdrawal becomes.
      </p>
      <h4>Will I be personally liable for the company's debts?</h4>
      <p>
        Not automatically. As a limited company director, you are generally
        protected from company debts. Personal liability only arises in specific
        circumstances, for example, if you signed a personal guarantee, made
        preference payments, or continued trading while knowingly insolvent in a
        way that worsened the position for creditors.
      </p>
      <h4>What is the difference between a winding up petition and a winding up order?</h4>
      <p>
        A petition is the legal application to the court — the beginning of the
        process. A winding up order is what the court issues if the petition
        succeeds. The order immediately places the company into compulsory
        liquidation, and the Official Receiver takes over. Between petition and
        order you still have options. Once the order is granted, you do not.
      </p>
    `,
